However, atrioventricular-sequential left ventricular pacing triggered by atrial leadless pacing impulse without right ventricular pacing has not been reported.

FIRST-IN-HUMAN/EARLY REPORTS SUMMARY: An 86-year-old man with complete heart block and cardiomyopathy received a dual-chamber leadless pacemaker (AVEIR DR) with WiSE left ventricular endocardial electrode on the septal wall. A novel "sync-to-pace" delay configuration enabled the atrial pacing impulse to trigger left ventricular stimulation, achieving a QRS duration of 142 ms.

DISCUSSION: This case demonstrates proof of concept for a fully leadless atrioventricular-synchronized system capable of delivering left ventricular septal endocardial pacing without right ventricular pacing dependency, offering a physiological pacing strategy for selected patients.

NOVELTY: First-in-human demonstration of an ultrasound-mediated left ventricular endocardial electrode triggered by an atrial leadless pacing impulse to deliver atrioventricular-sequential left ventricular septal stimulation without right ventricular pacing.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGE: This novel totally leadless architecture is a proof of concept for a more physiological pacing option for pacing-dependent patients while avoiding transvenous lead-related complications.

title: First-in-Human Axillary Vein Implantation of a Leadless Pacemaker: Breaking the Access Barrier.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Leadless pacemakers (LPs) are conventionally implanted transfemorally, with transjugular and subclavian routes reported as alternatives. Axillary access has not previously been reported.

FIH SUMMARY: A 78-year-old woman with chronic sacral wounds became temporary-pacing dependent following an inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. An LP was selected given infection risk. Because of a right femoral deep venous thrombosis, an abscess at the left femoral site, and restricted neck mobility limiting internal jugular access, she underwent left axillary vein implantation of an LP.

DISCUSSION: Axillary access served as a feasible alternative route. A septal position was achieved by rotating the delivery system counterclockwise, opposite the transfemoral direction, while a perpendicular sterile table supported the extracorporeal catheter length.

NOVELTY: This is the first reported axillary vein implantation of an LP.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGE: Axillary venous access is a feasible bailout route for LP implantation when femoral and internal jugular access are unavailable.

title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy.
summary: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

title: Atrial Cardiomyopathy Through the Pathologist's Lens: From Tissue Remodeling to Clinical Expression.
summary: Atrial cardiomyopathy (ACM) provides a useful framework for understanding structural, architectural, contractile, and electrophysiological disease of the atria. ACM and atrial fibrillation (AF) are closely linked but are not interchangeable: ACM favors arrhythmogenesis, whereas sustained AF can accelerate atrial injury. This review considers ACM from the pathologist's perspective, encompassing primary atrial disease and secondary remodeling associated with valvular disease and classical cardiomyopathies. The histologic spectrum includes cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and myocytolysis, interstitial and replacement fibrosis, endocardial fibroelastosis, adipose and inflammatory infiltration, vascular injury, and amyloid deposition. Structural remodeling is regionally heterogeneous, and appendage specimens may underrepresent abnormalities elsewhere in the atrium. Histologic interpretation requires attention to intrinsic regional architecture, associated lesions, previous interventions, and methods of quantification. At the molecular and cellular level, genetic susceptibility and acquired stressors converge on cardiomyocyte dysfunction, inflammation, fibroblast activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Correlating these tissue changes with mapping, imaging, biomarkers, and clinical outcomes will be necessary to validate noninvasive phenotypes and identify clinically meaningful disease subsets. At present, ACM should prompt etiologic investigation and risk assessment but does not by itself constitute an indication for specific therapy.

title: Multimodality Imaging in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: From Phenotyping to Precision Clinical Management.
summary: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disease characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy and a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from an asymptomatic phenotype to heart failure, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and advanced heart failure. Accurate diagnosis and risk stratification therefore require complex assessment. Multimodality cardiovascular imaging provides complementary structural, functional, and tissue characterization that cannot be obtained using a single imaging technique. Transthoracic echocardiography remains the cornerstone of initial diagnosis, hemodynamic assessment, and longitudinal follow-up, while advanced echocardiographic techniques provide additional information regarding myocardial and left atrial mechanics. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) has become central to phenotypic characterization and tissue assessment. Cardiac computed tomography offers complementary high-resolution anatomical information, particularly for coronary assessment and procedural planning, whereas nuclear imaging, provides insights into coronary microvascular dysfunction, myocardial perfusion, and selected phenocopies such as transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. Multimodality imaging also facilitates differentiation of HCM from other conditions such as athlete's heart, hypertensive heart disease, and infiltrative cardiomyopathies. Integration of imaging biomarkers with clinical and genetic information may improve prediction of adverse outcomes. Thus, multimodality imaging should be regarded not as a collection of competing techniques but as an integrated framework for precision diagnosis, risk stratification, therapeutic planning, and longitudinal management of patients with HCM.

title: Cellular consequences of non-ablative radiotherapy, a novel approach to ventricular tachycardias.
summary:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Radiotherapy (RT) with a single application of ionizing radiation (STAR) has been suggested as a non-invasive alternative to radiofrequency in ablating ventricular tachycardia (VT). Emerging data reveal that STAR may suppress VT without substrate destruction, by enhancing impulse conduction instead, through increased expression of NaV1.5 channels and connexin 43. The study aims to investigate electrophysiology and intracellular Ca2+ dynamics in cardiomyocytes (CMs) from mice subjected to in-vivo RT. The emerging data led us to evaluate biochemical changes potentially linking electrophysiological response to ionizing irradiation.

METHODS: CMs isolated 2 weeks after RT with low-dose (15 Gy) or high-dose (25 Gy) were compared to those of sham-treated mice (CTRL). We evaluated: i) the properties of the transient (INaT) and sustained (INasus) components of INa; ii) AP parameters, including the prevalence of Early After-Depolarizations (EADs); iii) intracellular Ca2+ dynamics; iv) CaMKII phosphorylation and v) ROS content.

RESULTS: 25 Gy RT i) increased INaT and, to a larger extent, INasus (increased INasus/INaT ratio); ii) increased AP amplitude, +dV/dtMAX and duration (APD) and facilitated EADs; iii) depressed intracellular Ca2+ dynamics. 15 Gy RT had similar but smaller effects (dose-dependency). 25 Gy RT reduced CaMKII phosphorylation but increased cell ROS content, thus providing a mechanism for the late component of INa (INaL) enhancement.

CONCLUSIONS: The results support the view that STAR may supress VT by increasing conduction velocity, with APD prolongation providing an additional mechanism. On the other hand, INasus enhancement and Ca2+ handling depression may impair electrical stability and contractility in the irradiated region.

title: Myocardial Fibrosis as an Arrhythmogenic Substrate: Integrating Genetics, Imaging and Invasive Electrophysiology for Sudden Death Risk Stratification.
Pre-Implant Substrate, Peri-Implant Electrical Features, and Outcomes Across Four Echocardiographic Phenotypes After CRT-D.
summary: Background: Reverse remodeling after cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillator backup (CRT-D) is heterogeneous and may reflect both pre-implant substrate and post-implant electrical response, with implications for subsequent outcomes. Objectives: This study evaluated a graded echocardiographic response framework after CRT-D as an integrative phenotype linking pre-implant substrate, peri-implant electrical features, and post-landmark clinical outcomes. Methods: The analytic cohort included 334 CRT-D recipients with complete four-group classification based on relative left ventricular end-systolic volume reduction at the first eligible post-implant echocardiogram. Baseline correlates of the 4-class response phenotype were assessed using ordinal logistic regression, supported by permutation-importance analysis. A stacked peri-implant model added ΔQRS, RV1SI pattern on ECG, left ventricular lead position, and lead depth. Time-to-event analyses used a landmark design anchored at the first post-CRT echocardiogram. Results: In the pre-implantation ordinal model, female sex (p = 0.005), higher baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (p = 0.032), left bundle branch block (p = 0.038), and dilated cardiomyopathy (p = 0.048) were associated with a more favorable response class. In the stacked peri-implant model, ΔQRS was the strongest correlate of higher response class (OR: 1.41; 95% CI: 1.15-1.73; p = 0.0008). Mortality differed across response classes (log-rank p < 0.001); compared with super-responders, negative responders had higher adjusted mortality (HR: 4.41; 95% CI: 1.82-10.70). At 60 months, heart failure hospitalization ranged from 23.3% to 2.9% and first appropriate ICD shock from 29.3% to 9.0% from negative responders to super-responders. Conclusions: After CRT-D, reverse-remodeling phenotype identified clinically distinct post-landmark risk profiles. Less favorable remodeling was associated with worse mortality, heart failure hospitalization, and appropriate ICD shock.

title: Novel SCN5A Variant in a Patient With Dilated Cardiomyopathy Complicated by Conduction Disorders and Recurrent Ventricular Arrhythmias.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Although sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 5 (SCN5A) was traditionally linked to electrophysiological disorders, growing evidence underscores its significant involvement in structural abnormalities.

CASE SUMMARY: A young dilated cardiomyopathy patient presented with a distinctive electro-structural dual phenotype, characterized by progressive left ventricular systolic dysfunction, conduction disorders, and concomitant severe ventricular arrhythmias. Comorbidities included coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea. Genetic testing identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense variant in the SCN5A gene. Comprehensive management included guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, antiarrhythmic agents, along with comorbidities management and risk factor modification.

CONCLUSIONS: This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of dilated cardiomyopathy in young patients with multiple overlapping etiologies-genetic, ischemic, metabolic. A de novo SCN5A variant may contribute to the arrhythmic phenotype and progressive cardiomyopathy.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Beyond its classical electrophysiological role, SCN5A is increasingly implicated in structural remodeling. This case emphasizes the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlation and gene-environment interaction.

title: Coexistance of Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity and Orthostatic Hypotension in Patients with Unexplained Syncope.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity (CSH) and orthostatic hypotension (OH) are established causes of syncope but are often considered separate entities. However, evidence suggests that CSH and OH may coexist and jointly contribute to syncope. This study investigates the relationship between CSH and OH in patients with unexplained syncope.

METHODS: A total of 1,908 patients aged ≥40 years (age, 63.7 ± 13.0 years; men, 45.3%) with unexplained syncope underwent carotid sinus massage (CSM) and head-up tilt testing (HUT). Occurrence of CSH in classical and delayed OH, including asystolic CSM responses was analysed.

RESULTS: Six-hundred-and-eighteen patients (32.4%, 68.9 ± 11.3 years) had OH, while CSH was present in 320 patients (16.8%, 72.2 ± 9.9 years), and was more common in patients with OH than without OH (24.1% vs. 13.3%, p < 0.001). Among patients with CSH, 46.6% also had OH. CSH occurred equally in both classical OH (62/275, 22.5%) and delayed OH (87/345, 25.2%). Among OH patients, CSH was associated with older age, male sex, lower supine diastolic blood pressure, hypertension, and syncope-related hospital admission. An asystolic CSM response was observed more often in OH patients (n = 42; 6.8%) compared with non-OH patients (n = 44, 3.4%, p < 0.001) and was associated with older age and lower resting heart rate.

CONCLUSIONS: CSH and OH frequently coexist in adults over 40 years evaluated for syncope. CSM may reveal a clinically relevant cardioinhibitory reflex in a subgroup of OH patients, supporting comprehensive cardiovascular autonomic testing in unexplained syncope.

title: Psychosocial Vulnerability and Immediate Emotional Triggers Preceding Sudden Cardiac Arrest.
Electrophysiological Manifestations of Suspected Bachmann's Bundle Infarction Due to Occlusion of the Right Sinus Node Artery.
